questions.question: What is the name of one of the earliest known written legal codes, famous for its principle of 'an eye for an eye'?
questions.explanation: King Hammurabi of Babylon created a set of 282 laws around 1750 BCE, carved onto a massive stone pillar.
questions.funFact: The code didn't just cover crimes; it also regulated trade, marriage, and even the minimum wage for workers!

questions.question: Which Macedonian king conquered the Persian Empire and created one of the largest empires of the ancient world by age 30?
questions.explanation: Alexander the Great spread Greek culture throughout the Middle East and parts of Asia before dying at a young age.
questions.funFact: He named over 70 cities after himself, and one city after his beloved horse, Bucephalus!

questions.question: What action by Julius Caesar in 49 BCE effectively ended the Roman Republic and started a civil war?
questions.explanation: By bringing his army across the Rubicon river into Italy, Caesar committed treason against the Roman Republic.
questions.funFact: When he crossed, he reportedly said 'Alea iacta est', which means 'The die is cast' – meaning there was no turning back!

questions.question: Which eastern continuation of the Roman Empire survived for a thousand years after the fall of Rome?
questions.explanation: The Byzantine Empire, with its capital at Constantinople, preserved Roman and Greek culture throughout the Middle Ages.
questions.funFact: They used a secret weapon called 'Greek Fire' in naval battles, which continued to burn even while floating on water!

questions.question: Who founded the Mongol Empire, which became the largest contiguous land empire in history?
questions.explanation: Genghis Khan united the nomadic tribes of the Asian steppe and conquered vast territories across Eurasia.
questions.funFact: The Mongols created a fast postal relay system called the 'Yam', allowing messages to travel across the empire incredibly quickly!

questions.question: During the Ming Dynasty, which Chinese admiral led seven massive naval expeditions to explore the Indian Ocean?
questions.explanation: Zheng He commanded a massive fleet of 'treasure ships' to establish trade and collect tribute for the Emperor.
questions.funFact: Some of his treasure ships were estimated to be over 400 feet long—more than four times the length of Columbus's ships!

questions.question: The capital of the Aztec Empire, built on an island in the middle of a lake, was called what?
questions.explanation: Tenochtitlan was a massive, highly organized city with canals, bridges, and giant pyramids.
questions.funFact: The modern city of Mexico City is built directly on top of the ruins of Tenochtitlan, and the lake has been mostly drained!

questions.question: During the Scientific Revolution, who proposed the heliocentric theory, stating that the Earth revolves around the Sun?
questions.explanation: Copernicus mathematically challenged the long-held belief that the Earth was the center of the universe.
questions.funFact: He delayed publishing his book until right before his death because he was afraid of the controversy it would cause!

questions.question: Which event is considered the starting point of the French Revolution in 1789?
questions.explanation: Angry citizens in Paris attacked the Bastille, a medieval fortress and prison, to seize weapons and gunpowder.
questions.funFact: At the time it was stormed, the famous 'prison' only held seven prisoners!

questions.question: Who led the only successful slave revolt in history, which resulted in the independence of Haiti?
questions.explanation: Toussaint L'Ouverture was a former slave who became a brilliant military leader, fighting off French, British, and Spanish forces.
questions.funFact: Haiti became the first independent nation in Latin America and the first post-colonial independent black-led nation in the world!

questions.question: The rapid modernization and industrialization of Japan in the late 19th century is known as what?
questions.explanation: Emperor Meiji was restored to power, and Japan rapidly adopted Western technology, military, and political systems.
questions.funFact: To learn about the West, the Japanese government sent a mission of scholars on a multi-year trip around the world called the Iwakura Mission!

questions.question: What 1884 meeting resulted in European powers dividing up the continent of Africa among themselves?
questions.explanation: During the 'Scramble for Africa', European nations drew arbitrary borders across Africa, largely ignoring existing cultural and ethnic boundaries.
questions.funFact: Not a single African leader was invited to the conference where their continent was divided!

questions.question: The assassination of which figure was the spark that ignited World War I?
questions.explanation: The assassination of the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne in Sarajevo led to a chain reaction of military alliances activating.
questions.funFact: The assassin, Gavrilo Princip, only got the chance to shoot the Archduke because the Archduke's driver took a wrong turn!

questions.question: Which political group, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized power in Russia during the October Revolution of 1917?
questions.explanation: The Bolsheviks overthrew the provisional government and established the first communist state.
questions.funFact: Lenin had been exiled in Switzerland, and the German government secretly transported him back to Russia in a sealed train to cause chaos!

questions.question: What 1929 event triggered the global economic collapse known as the Great Depression?
options: The end of World War I
questions.explanation: The sudden collapse of the U.S. stock market led to massive unemployment and poverty worldwide.
questions.funFact: In Germany, money became so worthless during the economic crisis that children used stacks of cash as building blocks!

questions.question: What physical barrier divided a major German city during the Cold War from 1961 to 1989?
questions.explanation: The Soviet-backed East German government built the wall to stop its citizens from fleeing to democratic West Berlin.
questions.funFact: Over 5,000 people managed to escape over, under, or through the wall, using everything from hot air balloons to zip lines!

questions.question: Who was the leader of the nonviolent resistance movement against British colonial rule in India?
questions.explanation: Gandhi used civil disobedience, such as boycotts and peaceful marches, to win India's independence in 1947.
questions.funFact: In 1930, Gandhi led a 240-mile march to the sea just to make salt, protesting a British tax on salt!

questions.question: Which war, lasting from 1950 to 1953, ended in an armistice but never an official peace treaty, leaving the country divided?
questions.explanation: The Korean War halted with a ceasefire, establishing a Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between North and South Korea.
questions.funFact: The DMZ is so heavily guarded and devoid of human activity that it has accidentally become a thriving nature preserve!

questions.question: What was the system of institutionalized racial segregation and discrimination in South Africa called?
questions.explanation: Apartheid was a policy enforced by the white minority government from 1948 until the early 1990s.
questions.funFact: Nelson Mandela, a key anti-apartheid leader, spent 27 years in prison before being released and becoming South Africa's first black president!

questions.question: Which major global pandemic killed tens of millions of people right after World War I?
questions.explanation: The 1918 influenza pandemic infected about a third of the world's population at the time.
questions.funFact: It is called the 'Spanish Flu' not because it started in Spain, but because Spain was neutral in WWI and their press was the only one freely reporting on the sickness!
